utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no preliminaries, then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could briefly make use of this time. It seems that we may have some unused hearing time tomorrow, so with a view towards trying to make full use of the time, the Chamber had asked me to address the Chamber with respect to 92 bis witnesses on Monday. I would be prepared to do that tomorrow. There are also some -- a proposition I'd like to make with respect to some of the documentary evidence with Monday's witness, perhaps we could discuss that, and Ms. Bibles would also like to address some of the concerns raised by Mr. Ivetic with respect to the late notice of exhibits. So if we could tentatively keep that in our minds for possible matter to be discussed tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we have time left tomorrow, that could certainly be used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are ready to continue -- Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off with 65 ter number 17992, and I'd like to go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it will be page 5 in the English in e-court at the top of the page, and page 7 in the Serbian in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, sir, for your information, this your article "Shame of Camp Omarska" that was published 7th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, it's page 5 in the English on the top page 7 in the Serbian in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, the selection I would like to ask you about begins as follows. It's actually the first full paragraph on that page: "Stories in Trnopolje, more freely told than in Omarska, are brimful of the squalid violence and black absurdity of civil war. There is a Sana, aged 13, who says: 'I was a fighter for the Muslims. They used to put us at the front when the fighting started. I was so scared that I ran away to the Serbian side of the village, to come here. I am still frightened, but I feel safer.'" First of all, sir, if you could help me out, is this the same 13-year-old that the ITN crew had filmed that talked about being -- used as used a human shield by the Muslim forces or is this another individual?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure, but I think it's the same one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Next, I'd like to go to the next paragraph in both versions of document, and the selection starts: "Then there was Igor, the Serbian soldier and guard whose uncle was killed last week and who says: 'I have my old school friends and my teacher in here [sic],' and then introduces his old pal Azmir, a professional footballer from behind the wire. 'I was taken here from Rizavanovci, after the fighting started,' says Azmir. 'There was some shooting from the Muslim side, then the police came and took the people away to clear the village of Muslims and to do the fighting.'" Do you remember these words, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember reporting them. I don't have a vivid recollection of the interview, but that is what the boy said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever had occasion to hear or research about a military tactic whereby civilians are evacuated from a combat area before combat is engaged with enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally or in this war?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Generally, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes, I'm sure it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that many occasions on which civilians were cleared during this part of the territory before they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that your information at the time was that Trnopolje centre was populated by civilians mainly, that is to say, persons that were believed not to have taken part in the armed uprising?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that both Trnopolje and Omarska were populated by civilians and people who had not taken part in the fighting, contrary to what we'd been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, again, we'll get to Omarska. I'm asking question, and I want answers to the questions I'd ask you, sir. So I would ask you to focus your answers and we'd get through this a lot quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if at the end you feel that by just limiting yourself to the answer -- the question as put to you that something important would have been lost, then, please, you'll always have an opportunity at the end of your testimony to address whatever matter in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you were told by the Serb authorities in Prijedor that Omarska for those persons who were suspected of having taken part in crimes or in being combatants and thus needed to be investigated and screened out from normal civilians?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there was a briefing in Omarska about various categories of prisoners, and we had also been guaranteed by Dr. Karadzic that there were no camps for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the -- you've mentioned the briefing. I'm not sure if we're going to get this. Let me ask you this way: Am I correct that persons found to be not involved in the military uprising were transferred from Omarska to Trnopolje, while those who were found to have committed crimes as part of the military uprising were sent to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite a complicated series of categories on which we were being briefed. To the best of my recollection, that was the idea or one of the versions that was given, that, yes, those who were found to have taken up arms would go to Manjaca as prisoners of war, and those who had not would be taken to Trnopolje. That did not accord with various other briefings in which I was told that people in Omarska were themselves prisoners of war, according to another account, but I think I've testified today -- sorry, yesterday, that there was nothing in -- at the time to indicate that the people in Omarska had been in any way combatants, and if I am permitted to talk about what has been found out subsequently, I now know them not have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'd like to limit your testimony to what you eye-witnessed, what you objectively saw. I don't want to talk about matters that you've researched and that you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Especially research that I have not been provided. That would be unfair, sir. Now, let's just finish up with Trnopolje and then move to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I'd like to play the footage from the -- from yesterday, the item that we had wanted to -- delayed for today to have a transcript. We have prepared a transcript and that has been -- the process of it started to put it into e-court, but of course documents cannot get into e-court within the time-period that we have this morning to try and get it in, so I've distributed hard copies, I believe, to all the booths and to opposing counsel, and I believe Madam Registrar has copies for the Judges, if that's accurate. And then with Your Honours's indulgence, I can play the first clip one time through and then play it again as per the procedure that we've now introduced into these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Ivetic, if you want the witness to limit himself to what he saw, then put questions and ask him what he saw instead of asking: Am I correct that persons found to be not involved...? You are not asking for any personal observation of the witness, and then later to say that it's unfair that he does seems not to be the best practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I did misspeak. I thought we were still talking about what had been told by the Prijedor officials as was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, read what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: May I proceed with the video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. If it is with text, we play it twice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, Your Honours, for the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic. That last speaker, I don't see his speech on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be -- I apologise, Your Honours. I don't have a copy of the transcript in front of me, but it should have translated the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll carefully look at it and listen to it in the second round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The two film crews visiting a humanitarian refugee centre in the village of Trnopolje, some 3 to 4 kilometres away from Omarska. The centre was mainly used by people in transit. They were trying to get away from the fighting and needed a place to stay during their travels. Our reporter, Mr. Bozanic, talked to some of these people who had escaped the war zone."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[VOICEOVER]: "Serbo-Croat 1st Speaker: First came those that didn't fight, that didn't ever fight. What do we have to fight for. "Serbo-Croat 1st Speaker: As soon as the shells started falling, we had to come. "Serbo-Croat Reporter: And what do you expect now? "Serbo-Croat 1st Speaker: That all the big shots step aside so they can live together again. "Serbo-Croat Reporter: What kind of status do you have here. Can you move ... are you free to move around? "Serbo-Croat 2nd Speaker: We can go and gather things and food from the neighbouring villages. "Serbo-Croat 3rd Speaker: They let us go ... to the villages. "Serbo-Croat 4th Speaker: I was lucky. I came with small kids. And I came with them from there, through the field. Nobody mistreated us. Nobody touched us. I was for 15 days in my village. My relatives were picked up and many of them have already reached Zagreb. Whoever had relatives, the majority would go to create Croatia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the sound quality is so poor that it is difficult to hear everything properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: French translation is finished. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I do note that the sound quality was low. It took us multiple times of listening through the tape to try and compile the transcript, and I believe there are still some portions that we could not fully make out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, am I correct that this individual, this reporter in here is one of the gentlemen that was accompanying the ITN crew and yourself with the Serb TV crew upon the visit to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely certain, but you introduced it yesterday, I think, as the footage having been shot by the crew which was part of our escort, some but not all of whom were in fatigues. But it's a little confusing -- a bit difficult to answer your question, because I notice that the compilation, the copyright, is dated 2000 to 2008, which is several years after the event, by emperorsclothes.com, and I've never heard of them. So I'm not exactly sure what's shot when and what's compiled when by who, but obviously this is put together in 2000 and 2008. But I -- the footage, originally, would have been shot by the Bosnian Serb crew, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I correct that this particular scene that we saw, this was the part of Trnopolje that was not fenced in where people could move in and out?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was one of the parts of the camp around the buildings where people were permitted to go and scavenge for food, yes. It wasn't the bit in which they were interned within that compound by the fence that we saw yesterday. There were various parts of the camp for different reason, as I've tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yesterday we talked about the comments of Dr. Stakic relating to the -- prior to you visiting Trnopolje. It would appear that these people here in Trnopolje were saying some of the same things as Dr. Stakic, would you not agree?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've tried to help the Court with this notion of Trnopolje as a confused and confusing place. These people in -- in the montage, posthumously, as I gather from the dates on it, put together - shot by the Bosnian Serb crew, do indeed cite people who appear to say some of the things that accord with what Mr. Stakic was saying, though I noticed that the man said he was in flight from shelling when he arrived and that accords, I think, perhaps with what I've heard from other people, there and since who have fled villages under shell fire. But in response to your question, given that this was put together in 2000, I think that to describe Trnopolje as a humanitarian centre after what I had gleaned that day and what we were given -- what we were actually given that day in the photographs showing emaciated torsos and people beaten black and blue, and they were given to us on the day and, indeed, before this Tribunal by the year 2008 or 2000. But that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If can interrupt you, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I could finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask about this: You said people. Wasn't there one photograph of one person that you received?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were more than one -- one person that gave us the film, but there are more than one person in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that from your testimony. We'll check. Now please put your answer.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, although it's somewhat innocuous, the practice of commenting on a witness's evidence we would object to. We would simply ask for the standard question/answer format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, what you remember and what you'll check is for you to decide and not to be communicated with the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we can go to the next clip, which is from 3 minutes and 46 seconds to 4 minutes and 34 seconds of part two of the original video. And Your Honours, again, this is a section that is subtitled but for which we did, apart from the subtitles, prepare a -- the transcript which starts on page 2 of the hard copy that was handed out, so I will play it through once through, beginning now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Second time through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[VOICEOVER]: Most of the people came here voluntarily, probably for food, and very often there was the issue of evacuation. You're from a big international organisation. Did you receive assistance? "No. Only for refugees from Croatia. "But since the fighting in Prijedor, people have the status of displaced persons, not that of refugees."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter again notes that the sound quality is very poor and it is difficult to verify the accuracy of the translation provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is on the record that the sound quality is very poor and difficult to verify. We'll see how to deal with that. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you recall this lady from the Yugoslav Red Cross being at Trnopolje when you visited the ITN crew?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not vividly, but I do recall her being there. She is from the Yugoslav, not the International Red Cross. Her point about -- that's why I noted her point about the international aid. The International Red Cross had been refused admission into Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of humanitarian aid sent from Serbia for these displaced persons at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, I didn't. We -- there was a medical centre in Trnopolje which I've described in previous testimony. Won't take your time with that now. But just to answer the question: The only aid, if that's the right word, that I was aware of at the time on the day was that which Dr. Merdzanic, who we saw in the video extract, and a lady vet helping him had managed to scavenge from houses from which people had fled in the village. The Yugoslav Red Cross was there, I do recall them and interviewed them. Indeed, they gave Omarska a clear bill of health and were happy with the state of affairs at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the question was focussing on humanitarian aid sent from Serbia, so the simple answer to that is that you are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unless some of the material they'd scavenged from these houses had come from Serbia, but I wasn't aware of the Yugoslav Red Cross providing any. Only that I've just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the question was not limited to the Red Cross. I think the initial question was humanitarian aid sent from Serbia by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever. Yes, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The last excerpt that I'd like to play is from the 7 minutes and 49 seconds to 9 minutes and 40 seconds of part 2 and is the first 59 seconds of part 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this section, Your Honours, is not subtitled. However, it is almost entirely in English except for a few utterances at the end. The transcript -- draft transcript that we have prepared last night from pages -- the middle of page 2 onward tries to incorporate both the transcript of the spoken English and a translation of the spoken B/C/S, or Serbo-Croat, and so I will now play it through the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now the second viewing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The quality seems to me already very poor, although --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what I read is -- at least comes close to the gist, apparently, of what is discussed, although I had great difficulties following it even in English. But let us play it, and with all the shortcomings and with all the reserves we may have as to the quality of the material of the transcript, and, therefore, necessarily, not because of our interpreters but of the translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Hello. "My name is Mehmed. "How did you come to be here? "I think it is very fine. Nothing wrong but it is very hot. "Do you sleep outside? "No, inside. "[Indiscernible] take you back and -- "No, it is very fine "You're fine? "Very fine. "How did you come here? You're a fighter? "With a bus. With a bus. "Are you a fighter? "No. "They came to your house and took you? "Yes. "Do you feel safe here? "I think it is very safe. But it's -- it's very hot. Other things that [indiscernible]. "But this man is very thin. "Yes, very thin, but, I think [indiscernible] -- is thin, all the people is not the same. Not the same. No, no, I think this person is a refugee. Not a prisoner. "[Indiscernible]. "I think it depends on the legal government. "Depends on the legal government. You cannot leave -- you cannot leave here? "No, not now. Not now. "Where are the women and children? "Gone. "Women and children in the house [indiscernible]. "Where are the women and children? "Gone. "The women in the house, other [indiscernible]. "What does this exist? "Yes. "[Indiscernible]. "It's a refugee camp "Where do you want to go? "Go home."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[VOICEOVER]: A voice coming from the background says: Tell them there's no food. A voice from the background: Look at the sight of him."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you would have been located with Ms. Marshall, who is the female reporter that was in this clip?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see me in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does this video-clip accurately depict what you recall this person in the blue overalls and those around him saying during this segment?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't hear all of this. These are the untransmitted ITN rushes, they must be, as disclosed in, I think, the Tadic case. I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move on to the next topic, can we seek to admit this video 1D259 into evidence with the caveat it should be marked for identification until the draft transcript is uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not oppose marking this video for identification purposes. We would, however, reserve our position on all materials from this web site until we've had an opportunity obtain a little more foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it comes from that web site or whether just the web site is mentioned in the material is not clear to me yet. Mr. Ivetic, any further information about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's -- well, it's my understanding that that's the web site that originally re-hosted this video in 2000. The -- it's dubbed in English, and my understanding is that there's B/C/S underlying the English and that this was broadcast on some TV in the region in the Balkans, probably closer to the events, but I've not been able to verify that yet and I will provide the Chamber with information as soon as I find more. Mr. Vulliamy has now said that this appears to be outtakes that would have been part of the Tadic proceedings. I do not know that. If that is the case, I will track it down via that means as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibit will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D259 becomes Exhibit D44, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And keeps that status and we expect more information from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would now like to switch gears and focus on Omarska and the time that you spent there as a fact witness. First of all, I would like to call up 65 ter number 17992 again. That would again be you are article written a couple of days after -- or published, I should say, a couple of days after you were at Omarska. And this time, I would like to look at the second page in English at something that Mr. Sebakoudin Anezovic [phoen] is reported to have told you in the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's in the middle of the page in English. And I believe it's also page 3 of the B/C/S. 17992 is the 65 ter number. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there I think we can see in the middle of the English towards the top, the section that starts: "I was in the defence force - but not caught in a fight. I tried to get to Trnopolje transit camp (a civilian camp) but the army caught me on the way and brought me here? "Sebakoudin, who shows no signs of beating, says, 'We are going investigated. Because I know that nothing can be hidden, I tell the truth and hope I will be okay. If I am guilty, then I'll have to face the consequences. I speak only of myself - personally, nobody touched me.'" And I think I may have had a missed end quote before "Sebakoudin says," -- before this section that says "Sebakoudin, who shows no sign of beating," and then it should be begin quotations for the remainder of it. Sir, do you recall this interview with this --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall talking with this man. Yeah. He was presented by the guards on our way in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When he mentions being part of a defence force, did you take that to mean he was part of the Bosnian Muslim Territorial Defence or TO in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have been that. Could have been a policeman in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: These words about Trnopolje transit camp, and especially the part "(a civilian camp)," are those your words or his?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be his.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could stay on the same page I'd like to ask you about another person that was detained at Omarska -- or excuse me, another person that you'd -- ah, here it is. I apologise. First, before we get to the other person that was detained, I think I found the discussion that you'd mentioned about the categories and that's on the same page where there's a person talking and I'd like to start off by reading it. It goes: "Omarska, they tell us, is an investigative centre for men suspected of being in the Muslim irregular army. They were [sic] rounded up or arrested, then screened to determine whether they are fighters or civilians." "Apart from their undernourishment and the humiliation of the drill, none of the 80 inmates we saw showed signs of violence or beating. "Those found to have prepared the rebellion go into category A, explains the police chief's spokesperson [sic] Nada Balban. There have been 126. They are awaiting trial. "Those found to be fighters are category B and go eventually to a prisoner of war camp at Manjaca, to which the Red Cross has been admitted (and to which the Serbian military were eager to steer us, rather than Omarska), and then to a military court. 'There have been 1.290.'" Now, first, sir, I want to ask you about the phrase here that you use, that the military were eager to steer to you Manjaca. In fact, sir, as -- if I can refresh your recollection, isn't it Colonel Arsic of the military that suggested he could authorise your visit to Manjaca because it was under the jurisdiction of the army, but if you wanted to go to these other camps you would have to talk to the civilian authorities? Isn't that a far more fairer representation of what transpired?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I my recollection is certainly that at the municipal headquarters in Prijedor, Colonel Arsic had offered to take us to Manjaca, but we wanted to go to Omarska. And it is correct, as you say, and I've testified many times. He then handed us over to the other people in -- on his committee with regard to our trip to Omarska because, as you say -- as you quote, and you say, the Red Cross had visited Manjaca but not Omarska and that was our reason for wanting to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And now I'd like to ask you about an individual that you interviewed in Omarska. Do you recall the individual who had injuries to his face that reported that he had fallen and that the injuries were self-induced?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may fast forward, am I correct that you ran into this man years later when he was a member of the Bosnian Muslim army in the advance on Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him again by pure coincidence in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for purposes of the record, this is the 16th September 2002 Stakic transcript, which is P199 in our case. This is transcript page 7941 of that day and is the 44th page in e-court where the witness talks about this. For the sake of efficiency, I will only ask a question as I do not think I need to have the quote up, but by all means, if -- if you think -- if the other side thinks we need to have the transcript up it can be put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the question that I have that was unclear to me, sir, when you talked about meeting this man at or near Donji Vakuf, was he -- you mentioned a Bosnian military commander that was leading the advance on Donji Vakuf. Is that this individual or was he one of the other soldiers that was present?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was one of the other soldiers and he was able to tell me a bit more about the wound that he said had happened because he had fallen over. It wasn't at all he'd been very, very badly beaten and had been in the meantime treated for damage to his brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you also say that he, I believe, in that section of the Stakic case, that he had regained weight. If I can try and have you go back in time to 1992 when the Prijedor officials were talking to your group, did they tell you of food shortages that were being caused by the war and that were being experienced by all persons in the region of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did say some things about food shortages, but they were -- appeared to be not affecting everybody equally and did not explain the skeletal state of Mr. Velic, who is the man at question, when I met him in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not totally irrelevant in this context is that the words in the Stakic transcript are "he had put on an awful lot of weight by then." Not "he had gained weight." "He had put on an awful lot of weight." So therefore, if you do not show the relevant portion on the screen, please be very precise in your quotations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I'm just trying to move along as quickly as possible to finish the witness in the time that I promised I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you can do that -- I mean, by misquoting, you are, as a matter of fact, we're losing time. And in preparing -- I'm not inviting you to have it on the screen. I am inviting you to carefully prepare and give a quote which is accurate, and that doesn't take any time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At yesterday's transcript, page 2594, lines 22 through 25, you seemed to dismiss the meal served at Omarska saying: "If that's what you could call it." Was that a comment on the quality of the meal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quality, quantity, and the apparent desperation with which they devoured it, which suggested that they had not seen much food, if any, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone mention to you at that time that the kitchen that prepared food for Omarska prepared that same food to feed the Bosnian Serb police and the Bosnian Serb army in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's -- they didn't, no. And if they did, the guards were certainly getting food from some other source than the prisoners. Besides, they were in pretty good shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have already mentioned Mr. Drljaca and Ms. Balaban [phoen] from the police. Am I also correct that you were introduced to a Mr. Mijakic [phoen] who was introduced to you as the commander of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were introduced to Mr. Mijakic as the commander of the guards at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vulliamy, am I correct that Mr. Mijakic was also from the Prijedor police structures?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which structure he was part of, actually. He was -- he had a beret on. He was wearing fatigues. I didn't and really don't know which structure he was. But he appeared to be answering to Mr. Drljaca, but I don't know exactly what chain of command he was under. I still don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's fair enough. Now I'd like to move to another topic. Am I correct that the Serb authorities gave you a list of suspected sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina where camps were said to be operated by the other sides to the conflict and meant for Serb detainees?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such a list came from two sources. One was Dr. Karadzic himself and the other was from his deputy, Nikola Koljevic, during a rather strange tea we had after we found the camp, when he was sort of jeering at the west, generally, for having taken so long to find them and challenged us to look for the others on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that one of the locations that was given to you was Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And I took, as it were, that -- that the point that both these men were making seriously, and if I may just -- just go back to a question you asked me yesterday about sort of doing all the right things for my career and so on, I actually did not take up the opportunity to go and bask in our discoveries at Omarska and Trnopolje but went directly over to the other side, which took some time, in order to investigate Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say we went over to the other side. Dretelj was -- at the first time, you actually visited twice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Once in 1992 on the occasion I'm talking about now, and then again in either late 1993 or early 1994. I think late 1993. There were different lots of prisoners in the camp each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The first time you went to Dretelj it was operated by the HOS paramilitary group under the auspices of the Croat -- Bosnian Croat forces and Serb detainees were being held there, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, including women Serbian detainees, and we revealed the atrocity of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the second time you visited, it was now no longer the HOS but other Bosnian Croat forces holding Bosnian Muslim detainees, and that would have been the time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was then transferred under the authority of the HVO, the Bosnian Croat army, and the inmates were, for the most part anyway, Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the first part of my question here, I'd like to focus on the first visit that you had, I believe, around 15 August 1992, give or take a few days.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's mid-August 1992, yes. It's immediately after we found the camps, given the time it took to go round the very long way to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you first had to go and see Mr. Mate Boban, leader of the Bosnian Croat faction, in his office in Grude?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to 1D00240.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is the transcript of the witness's testimony in the Prlic proceedings before the ICTY. I'd like to call up page 31 in e-court. This is transcript page 1504 and this section starts at line 18 and goes on to the next page to line 10. And, sir, here I begin with the question that was posed to you: "Q. Let me return to something that you said a few minutes [sic] ago. This is reflected on page 26, lines 13 and 14 of the transcript. "You told us that this meeting was 'at his office in a town called Grude, a small town and quite a menacing place.' "Again, that's lines 13 and 14 of page 26 of today's transcript. Can you elaborate, sir, upon what you meant by 'a menacing place'? "A. Well, I mean, both in -- both in this war and in previous wars I got used to places where I didn't feel comfortable. I didn't feel threatened. And let's put it that although there was no fighting, there was the odd rasp machine-gun fire into the sky. There were some very heavy lads around who weren't giving us very welcoming looks. The -- I didn't particularly like the fact that the portrait of Ante Pavelic, who was the Ustasha dictator in the Second World War, was in the windows of some of the shops, nor did I find it very tasteful that the U - a sort of capped U - of that movement had been painted on some of the walls. "I didn't feel that I -- that I was at risk, but it was an uncomfortable place to be, and it was an intimidating place and a heavily militarised one, although it was nowhere near any front line." Sir, do you recall this testimony from Prlic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And of course, I recall Grude as you've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does it still accurately comport to your recollections of Grude?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yesterday we talked about Mr. Stakic's speech where he talked of fears on the parts of Serbs due to their memories of World War II. Was the return of the Ustasha movement one the fears expressed by the Serb officials in Prijedor that you had met with one week prior to meeting with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did talk about their experiences during the Second World War and we discussed this at length, actually, during an extraordinary conversation with Dr. Kovacevic who we met that day in 1992 who did make these recollections in 1996 when I talked to him, where he refined very interestingly, and very regretfully, some of the points he'd made in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Am I also correct that the list given to you by the Serb authorities included two locations at Tarcin and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Konjic? Konjic I think was on the list. Tarcin, definitely, because I went to Tarcin to try and investigate that as well. It was a tunnel and I couldn't find anything when I went. It had either not existed or had been cleared by the time I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to find out that right now in the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they are in the middle of prosecuting eight Bosnian Muslims precisely in the case of Mustafa Djelenovic -- Djelilovic and others, case number S1 1 K 007914 KRI precisely for alleged crimes relating to not one but three detention camps in Tarcin that held Serbs, including in a silo, in a school, and in army barracks, torturing them continuously from 1992 through February 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would I be surprised? No. If it's -- if the trial is taking place, the trial is taking place. Why would I be surprised?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you found no evidence of that? You didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there, I didn't see any of the tunnel that I endeavoured to -- to get to, and then having -- other things were happening, I -- perhaps I should have looked harder. We did Dretelj instead and we did pages 1 to 3 at Dretelj and the appalling conditions of the Serbian prisoners there. One couldn't go to all the camps and nor did we try to go to all the camps on the Bosnian Serb side. It would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One last --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't surprise me, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One last question before, I think, we have the break: What about Konjic, did you ever have occasion to follow-up on or investigate Konjic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're at the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are at break. Mr. Ivetic, you made a great effort in giving the case number and all kind of details of that case. Are you going to do something with that or is it -- I mean, is it give the witness further leads to what he could look at or is it for the Chamber or?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's to identify the proceedings to give as much information as possible to the witness to see if he was aware of that proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if -- I guess we could also get paperwork from that case, if Your Honours are interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying that. We'll take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00, but not until after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to deal with a few matters. Scheduling for next week. The Prosecution has requested that the order of the first two witnesses scheduled for next week be reversed. The Defence does not oppose to this switch and the Chamber allows it. Could the Prosecution already start thinking about what it wants to do with the nine documents which were announced to be tendered as associated exhibits in the Rule 92 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was going to address that at the end of redirect once I could see which documents have been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll wait for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready you may proceed

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the other location we mentioned in Bosnian Serbs where Serb authorities said that Serbs were being held by Muslim forces, Konjic: Do you agree with me that at the time you didn't know but now you know that place to be called by a different name, Celebici?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was there a location called Lara in Split, Croatia, included on the list, if you know? And did you know anything about that location? Lara.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that one, no. I'm sorry. I'm sure if it was on the list, well and good. I don't remember it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, if there's any need to correct anything, it's not by speaking aloud. Especially because your microphone is not switched on so it would be lost for the record anyhow. Please take off your earphones say it at a low volume to one of the team members and then, of course, the Chamber appreciates your active participation and your contribution to the accuracy of the proceedings. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to move to another topic that you've already alluded to, the fact that you returned to Prijedor to interview some of the Serb officials again. Am I correct that this was in February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The officials you interviewed included Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic and, I believe, that the transcript from the Stakic proceedings that has been introduced into evidence goes into detail about your interviews of these individuals at that time. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript of the Stakic case does -- I think, goes into -- is verbatim, the conversation with Dr. Stakic. As I recall, there is -- yes, and there is some consideration of the Kovacevic interview as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you neglected to introduce yourself by your real name to either Dr. Stakic or Dr. Kovacevic when you met and interviewed them in February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was afraid to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you give them a fake name?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think I was asked for one. It -- I -- I just said I was from a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I also correct that the meeting with Mr. Kovacevic was not recorded on tape, as the 1992 meetings had been?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was myself and another print reporter from the "New York Times."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As far as the meeting with Dr. Kovacevic is concerned, am I correct that Kovacevic drank homemade Slivovitz brandy throughout the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout most of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long did that meeting last?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say about between an hour and an hour and a quarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you drink alongside him or did you just symbolically take one sip but not keep pace with him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't keep pace with him. I had between a sip and a quarter of a glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me Kovacevic consumed seven to eight shots in that span of an hour or an hour and a quarter that included most of the bottle?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the Stakic transcript, which, again, is Exhibit P199 in these proceedings, at page 228 in e-court, which is the transcript page T8125 from 17th September, 2002, you agreed that -- that Dr. Kovacevic was at least -- at least was definitely was not sober but that you would hesitate to call him intoxicated from the brandy at the time that you questioned him. Does that -- and we can wait for the page to come up, if you'd like to -- and it's at page 228. It should be near the bottom, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's at lines 19 and following "not sober" at line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly wasn't sober. He was coherent, however. Admirably so. It was an extremely interesting conversation during which he was estimably candid. So he wasn't intoxicated inasmuch as he couldn't string a sentence together, but he certainly wasn't sober either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You tasted the brandy. Was it potent?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That stuff usually is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that immediately after you completed the meetings and interviews in February of 1996 with Drs. Kovacevic and Stakic, at which time you did not advise them of your identity, you sent a CD with your notes of these meetings to a Mr. Keegan whom you knew very well at the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent a memorandum and some notes to Mr. Keegan, who I didn't know that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I say you knew him because you met with him immediately prior to going to Prijedor to interview these individuals without giving your real name.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with him before I went. I can't remember how long before I went it was, but it wasn't immediately. And as I say, I didn't give my name to them because I was scared. I didn't have authority to be there and these men didn't have any reason to particularly like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could try to refresh your recollection, sir, we have been provided with a proofing -- excuse me, a statement, interview -- interview information sheet evidencing that you were interviewed at the ICTY 16th January 1996. Would that be immediately prior to going to Prijedor in February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about a month before. Because I remember the day after the interviews we got back to Zagreb and it was St. Valentine's day, so that would put it a month before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Keegan and the Prosecution at that time not only wanted you to be a witness, they wanted you to be one of their key experts to establish the element of widespread and systematic crimes by Serbs including Drs. Kovacevic and Stakic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly that they were after Kovacevic and Stakic. I was helping Mr. Keegan with the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can focus on the chronology a little bit. Am I correct that you first met with the Office of the Prosecutor and with Mr. Keegan personally on 18th April, 1995, in Washington at your office?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date but it was in Washington, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then you met with -- with the representatives of the ICTY again, as you mention, in January, about one month before going to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think by then they were established here in The Hague. I'm not sure they were in -- in the previous year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time that you went to Prijedor in February of 1996 and interviewed these gentlemen, Drs. Stakic and Kovacevic, did you at any time identify yourself as someone who had met with the Prosecution for purposes of preparing to be a Prosecution witness or perhaps an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. I was preparing an article for the newspaper. Which I wrote and was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time advise either of these men of their rights as suspects of Tribunal investigation, including the right to be represented by counsel or the right to refuse to answer any of your questions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A journalist doesn't do that and I didn't, no. I wanted to find out who they were and what they thought about all the things that we'd discussed that day when we I had met them and the things that had emerged since then about Omarska, Trnopolje, and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you consider your conduct in interviewing them in February 1996 under these conditions to be objective as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered it to be necessary to -- to -- to getting the story in the extremity of the situation and given what, by then, I knew to be the record of extreme violence in the area and in those camps, in particular. I wasn't any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I ask you again, would you consider your conduct in interviewing them in February of 1996, without giving your real name, without advising that you had been consulted twice to be an expert witness for the Office of the Prosecution, would you consider that conduct by yourself to be objective as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I considered it the only way I was going to get them to talk about what had happened in 1992, the last time we'd met. I think if I'd declared myself as the person they met in 1992, I may have been arrested, I may well have been physically harmed or worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you consider your actions to have been undertaken neutrally or were you being partial at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're splicing the words again here. I've already tried to explain to the Court that I think by this time I had followed up, to the best of my abilities, professionally the -- the -- the -- what -- that which had been hidden from us that day in August 1992. We knew an awful lot more by the time I went back to talk to these men. I thought it was certainly worthy and in the public interest to get their account of what they thought had been happening, and I think if I had declared who I was, I would have, A, not heard their accounts; and probably put myself in extreme danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, this is not really an answer to the question, I would think. The question was whether the actions undertaken, whether you considered them to be neutrally or you being partial at the time. And I did understand the question to say, well, if you first meet with the Prosecution and then go to someone you had interviewed earlier and further interview him, not telling that person that you had been consulted by the Prosecution, whether that makes you, in your own view, a partial person or whether you could still be neutral under those circumstances. Is that the question you had on your mind, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whether you had fear to, say, to present yourself under your own name is a different matter compared to this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes, I'll be more specific: Objective, yes; neutral, not necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consider that your interviews at this time were accomplishing a job that would be beneficial to the prosecution of these men before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was, that was a secondary consideration. I thought that what I was getting in those discussions was a -- it was extremely enlightening on the pressing matter of the worse violence in Europe for half a century, which is in the public interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please call up 65 ter number 1D00236 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, sir, this is a two-page information report from the Prosecution relating to another meeting you had with them, this time in 2001. Do you recall having a meeting with members of the staff of the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in 2001?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this specific meeting, but I do recognise the name of the submitter as he is called at the top. He did come to interview me on a case, and I recognise some of the names below. Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put to you the subject matter of the meeting and see if that refreshes your recollection of this meeting, and I'll start with the first and second paragraphs. "During a meeting with Mark Harmon Nicola Piecente and Ulrich Musselmeyer, I was briefed by Mark Harmon to meet with Edward Vullimay and hand in a copy of the Plavsic-Krajisnik indictment and to request that he reads the document and gives consideration to ways that the defendants could be linked alleged crimes. Harmon briefed me that Vulliamy may well have 'insider' knowledge that may assist us in showing the linkage. He also may be able to identify persons with a closer political perspective who that Vulliamy could contact on our behalf with a view to assisting us. "When I met with Vulliamy, I handed him a copy of the indictment and worked through the document with him. He discussed links that he could establish between Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, down to Milutinovic and Arsic [sic] of the Banja Luka and Prijedor military respectively, and down through Kovacevic, Stakic, Drljaca, and Mikic connected, he states, to Omarska and Trnopolje." And now, sir, I'll ask you: Does this refresh your recollection of a meeting that you had in 2001 with members of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the date again --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at the top, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very soon after 9/11 in New York on which I worked a lot. I don't recall the specific meeting, and you'd have to ask Mr. Tait-Harris about when and -- exactly when and where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he did come to New York. I don't remember the other people being there. I don't remember this. I played no role in the -- the cases involving Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik. Insider knowledge is his term, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- did you offer them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first try to avoid any confusion. You said you don't remember the others being there. Now, if I read this document, and that's always the risk of looking at the document for the first time, it is that the author of the document met - that is, Jonathan Tait-Harris - met with Mark Harmon, Nicola Piecente, and Ulrich Musselmeyer, and that he subsequently - he, as far as I read here - alone met with Mr. Vulliamy where he gives no date for that meeting, so if it would have been the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It would have been prior to this document, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore it seems that perhaps having had only a glance to the document, you may have been confused as to with whom you are supposed to have met. Apart from where.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's why I said in 2001, because I don't know the exact date when would you have met with this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. Rereading it, I see too that that's what's happening. Certainly I'm not having anything to do with The Hague at this time of 2001. At late in November. But, yes, I did meet with Mr. Tait-Harris in New York but not these other people regarding these cases or this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you say it was soon after 9/11. The date of this document is 5/11/2001. We always have to be very careful whether it's the 11th of May, or the 5th of November, but both not -- well, soon after 9/11 could be, if you make "soon" two months, but it could have also been before. I do not know what notation of dates is used. But I do understand that you now have a recollection of having met Mr. Tait-Harris?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was that before or after 9/11, or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would then put this in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact I'm pretty sure it was before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would then put this in May rather than in November. At least --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the American dates, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least if the date of the document follows the meeting soon. I do not know how much time Mr. Tait-Harris may have taken to author this information report. Let's try by carefully reading every single letter to avoid misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think can I clarify things easily, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you can. Until now, at least, the witness was confused. That's for sure. About with whom he was supposed to have met.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I met with Mr. Tait-Harris in New York. I don't recall much about that meeting. And the others I didn't meet in the same room at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, with regard to this meeting that you say was in -- that you say was in May, you also had another meeting in November 2011 with the Office of the Prosecutor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do tell me? I don't know. November 2000 and?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You testified in the Karadzic case at 9 November 2011.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were briefed -- or you were proofed by the Office of the Prosecutor on 7th/11 -- 7th of November, 2011, does that refresh you recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can get back to this document, sir. Did you in fact provide advice or strategy to the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just stop you again. I think the name of the case which you mentioned in which the witness was proofed, I take it due to quick speaking, is missing in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That would be the Karadzic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Karadzic proceedings in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 11th November, 2011. That would have been case number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 2011, correct. And the proofing was the 7th of November 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear and it's also clear now in what context Mr. Vulliamy met.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... there was confusion because apparently the witness understood it to be November 2000 but it's clear now that it was 2011. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now just to be absolutely clear, my questions are relating to the -- what we've established now as the May 11th meeting with Mr. Jonathan Tait-Harris. Did you in fact at that time provide advice on strategy to the Office of the Prosecution on how to prosecute Serb defendants?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been called in a number of trials and have testified to the Office of the Prosecutor what I know. I was not called in either the trial of Mrs. Plavsic or Mr. Krajisnik. This term "insider knowledge" is Mr. Tait-Harris's. I'm not aware that I had any or have any regarding Plavsic and Krajisnik, and if I had, they didn't see it as of any use to them because I wasn't called in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, sir: Was there -- did the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY Tribunal have a case against Milutinovic, Arsic, or Mikic, or are those names that you suggested and provided advice on how to link them to crimes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they this cases against those people, and I wasn't offering names for perspective indictments. Certainly not, sir. I work for a newspaper. Not for -- not for this Tribunal. I testified at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that Mr. Jonathan Tait-Harris is untruthful when he is saying here: "He discussed links that he could establish between Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, down to Milutinovic and Arsic [sic] of the Banja Luka and Prijedor military respectively, and down through Kovacevic, Stakic, Drljaca, and Mikic, connected, he states, to Omarska and Trnopolje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to intervene at this moment. Discussing links does not tell us who first mentioned the names. And you're putting to Mr. Vulliamy that Mr. Jonathan Tait-Harris is untruthful when he says he discussed links. The issue that was raised in the present examination of Mr. Vulliamy was: Did you give him the names or did he suggest the names to you. That's at least how I understood it. If I misunderstood, please clarify, Mr. Ivetic, together with the witness. But I think the suggestion that by saying "he discussed," that it also means that he came up with the names seems not to be automatic and logically compelling. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, prior to this time you had met with the Office of the Prosecutor twice, in April of 1995 and in January of 1996. At that time, they had discussed using you as an expert witness to prove widespread and systematic behaviour that could be linked to crimes. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had been called as a witness, I think, in 1998 as well, so I'd met with them more than twice, between -- before the date of this memorandum. And I had been called in, I think, the case of Mr. Kovacevic which, to the best of my recollection, was 1998. And all these names would have been in my notebook, in my evidence, in the case of Dusko Tadic and the case of Mr. Kovacevic, Dr. Kovacevic, and perhaps, Your Honours, I could, as it were, resolve this matter by saying that's where the matters came from. They were in evidence. They were out there anyway and in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are still with the last question, whereas Mr. Ivetic expected an answer to his next question: Whether, in those first meetings, April 1995, January 1996, whether the Office of the Prosecution had discussed with you to use you as an expert witness to prove widespread and systematic behaviour that could be linked to crimes. So it's the subject of the discussions in 1995/1996.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't being asked to -- to discuss any -- any -- any links - his word - or any insider knowledge - his word. When I'm called by the Office of the Prosecution, I -- I give my evidence. I -- I don't understand, actually, what I'm being asked. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'll repeat it to you. What Mr. Ivetic asked you is the following: When you met in April of 1995 and January 1996, and what was the subject matter of the discussion? Did that include a possible role for you as an expert witness? I leave it to that at the moment. Was that discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: April 1995, if that's when it was, I can't remember. Oh, sorry. April 1995. Yes. It was to discuss my role as an expert witness in the Tadic case. Sorry. January 1996, likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And your expertise or your testimony would be about the widespread and systematic behaviour of -- that you had observed. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked to give an impression -- to give my overview of the entire war and the visit to the camps we have been discussing today and yesterday for -- to the Tadic Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to this document that's still on the screen, sir. If I can ask you about, did the Office of the Prosecutor, as is reflected here, and I'll read -- well, let me read what Mr. Jonathan Tait-Harris has written so we are clear. In the first paragraph, which again is talking about his discussions or preparations prior to meeting with you, he says: "He also may be able to identify persons with a closer political perspective who that Vulliamy could contact on our behalf with a view to assisting us." Did the Office of the Prosecutor ask you to contact persons on their behalf to assist them in prosecuting Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall. And if they did, I didn't. Because I wasn't in a position to contact people on their behalf, nor do I contact people on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page of this document, the second paragraph from the top. "With regards to forcible transfer, he recommended the use of his colleague Ian Traynor, of 'The Guardian' newspaper, who was well-informed on these matters." Did you provide or recommend the use of your colleague Ian Traynor of "The Guardian" newspaper for the Office of the Prosecutor to assist them to prosecute Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may well have put them on to Ian, yes, because he did a lot of work on Kozarac and around that time and area, but he is not a Bosnian Serb. He is a colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the Bosnian Serb comes in from, sir, but I did not intend to imply that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be that it was misunderstood. The question was "did you," but I don't think whether you said "recognise," or "would you," maybe "did you recommend" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Recommend, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- "the use of your colleague for the Office of the Prosecutor to assist to prosecute Serbs." That may have been misunderstood, that last portion, and may have caused the confusion. I think the witness has answered your question. The question, however, was composite. It was first a recommendation to use a person; and the second part of the question was, whether this was for the purpose of prosecuting Serbs. When you may have mentioned the name of your colleague, was it in the context of assisting the Prosecution to prepare Prosecutions of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- it would only have been that, yes. Maybe Mr. Traynor knew something I didn't. I can't actually remember which case we were discussing at this point with Mr. Tait-Harris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you gave that information, you thought that Mr. Traynor would have available information which might assist the Prosecution in their intended prosecutions, which you understood to be prosecution of Serbs at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be that I was asked a question I didn't know the answer to or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I hope I assisted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at the last paragraph of this document which is already on the screen, the part that I wanted at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONATHAN TAIT-HARRIS SAYS
utterances.text: "The indictment was left with Vulliamy to allow him to give it further consideration. I asked him if he was able to provide any information concerning events in Sarajevo. He stated he could give general information available from a number of sources, such as random shelling, shootings, and the terrorising of the population." And that's the end of the quote I'd like to ask you about. Is it true that you offered information from many sources to the Office of the Prosecutor relating to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least a number of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A number of sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, so we're discussing Sarajevo at this point. I don't remember. It's best to ask Mr. Tait-Harris. I don't remember offering, sort of general sources. I see that I'm -- I -- I do give him an account of the Dobrinja water line shelling which I was a witness to, or at least the immediate aftermath of. But I don't recall giving him a list or -- or anything. I don't actually recall reading the indictment, I regret to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document, 65 ter number 1D00236 as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D236 becomes Exhibit D45, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D45 the document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for your answers to my questions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto would have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, this morning you were asked questions about Trnopolje, and in one of your answers you said that it was a confused and confusing place and that you -- you -- there were areas which were not fenced in and there were others which were fenced in. What I would like to ask you is: Did you get an opportunity to visit all the parts of Trnopolje, including the fenced-in parts?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. We did get the opportunity to tour the not -- not fenced in or partially fenced bits of the camp which are to the side where the buildings were essentially. And here was this -- and I'm sorry to put it in such vague language, this mixture of people with a mixture of reasons for being there, as I tried to establish.
