Some in flight, some corralled on buses. Others had come of their own accord. We did not get to be inside the fenced-in compound that you can see us filming through the fence into, if that's clear. There's this bit which has fencing on three sides, one of which is the barbed wire fence, with a wall at the back. That's the compound under guard and fenced off where the men had come that morning, we understood, from Keraterm. And we were not -- we were not permitted to go inside that area, but we were able to move and talk -- sometimes with the guards following us, sometimes not, in the area which was not fenced off or partially fenced off around the buildings. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apart from those two parts, the partially fenced in and the one that is fenced in with barbed wire, were you aware of any other parts of the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh. I mean, I didn't know then and I don't know now whether we saw, you know, every corner of it, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know you haven't seen every corner of it. You have just told us you didn't have permission to get into the barbed wire, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you were you aware of any other part of the camp other than these two parts?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At this now -- at this moment now, are you aware?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were some rooms which had been mentioned during this work I've been doing for the new book where there were -- there were -- the places that have been mentioned where beatings and violations took place that I now know I did not visit in 1992, yes. I mean, I now know that we didn't see all -- all of the camp. I now know that we didn't see all of the camp that -- of the -- of the buildings. We didn't go into all the rooms, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you told anything about the purpose or purposes of those parts of the camp that you didn't visit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you given the purpose of those parts later?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I've gone over this in some detail and at length with many of the survivors and the people who were in the camp, the former internees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what were the purposes of those other parts?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the rooms I believe were used for the violation of girls and women, and there were rooms which were used for beating prisoners, including the one or two that we -- of which we were given the photographs on the day, and that is in -- in research that I've done during the 20 years since and others can testify who were actually in them if they are called in this trial. But I -- I have been told about places in Trnopolje where the violations and the beatings took place, but we didn't visit on the day, yes, since, but those are places that I did not know about when we went in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just give me one second. Judge Fluegge has a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we heard in the video and during your examination that some of the detainees were allowed to go to surrounding villages to get some food. Did anybody tell you that it was possible to leave the camp and to go somewhere else, despite these cases of gathering food in the surrounding villages; for instance, to go back to their homes or to other places in the former Yugoslavia or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Again, it's a bit -- it's -- it's quite a complicated answer, if you'll forgive me. Yes, I have spoken to people who were able to go foraging for food in the village of Trnopolje, most of the Muslims and very few Croats in that village having been forced to leave their homes, they were empty, and people could go back to -- to get food out of them. The doctor and vet that I've mentioned also went round the houses looking for medicines, basic aspirin, and so on. I've never met anyone who escaped from Trnopolje, as it were, who made the run, which I think you've asked about. But people were able to make, as it were, authorised visits back to their villages. I've interviewed at great length the vet on a number of occasions over the years, and she was able to, for instance, go back to Kozarac to pick up people who had been left after the shelling. She refers in particular to a blind old man, to a badly disabled old lady who actually was dead by the time they got there. So there is movement, but I've never met anyone who told me that they'd, as it were, left the camp, got away, gone home, and made it to Croatia on their own in safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that those who were permitted to go to their homes or other places in the surrounding villages to get some food or medicine, that they all had to come back to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my very strong impression that if they didn't they'd be in trouble of some kind. And it's also -- it was my impression on the day that we visited - and confirmed since - that it would have been extremely dangerous for them to have been moving unauthorised across country as a -- as a -- as it were, if you like, an ex-detainee of Trnopolje. That if they did, they would be likely to be apprehended and shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. My first question is directly related to the questions Judge Fluegge asked you. In Trnopolje, as I understand, there were men, there were women, there were children. Now, those who were allowed to go back to their homes, could that be men, possibly a wife which was with them, if there were any families, as such, and the children, so that the whole of the family could return to their home to get food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They were and would have been. Some food was able to be delivered as people arrived progressively while others had stayed at home, but again, just to -- to continue my answer to -- to Justice Fluegge. The -- I mean, there was a case which I've interviewed and reported of somebody who decided to go home, having been released from Keraterm to Trnopolje, went home to join his family in the house and they were all murdered. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them. So, yes, but it was extremely dangerous of them -- for them to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was that were there families, that is, husband, wife, and children, detained in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In their entirely -- in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If someone was allowed to go home, a man, for example, or a woman, would that person be allowed to take his wife or her husband and the children and to go home all together, or would one member of the family be allowed to go home or do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But it's possible. And I don't know of any family that did, as it were, you know, leave in its entirety to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say you cannot confirm neither deny that this -- that whole families [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I can't. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have one question, also a follow-up question to the questions put to you by Judge Moloto. Judge Moloto asked you whether there were other parts, and then you described that you had had no access to the buildings, on the basis of adjudicated facts, this Chamber accepts without further evidence that among the buildings was a school, a two-storey school, and a building which was known as the -- as a -- the Dom, including a theatre, kind of a community building. When you said you had no access to rooms, are you referring to rooms in those buildings, or were they elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. Your Honour, the -- the -- yes, I agree there were these two principal buildings, the school and the Dom cultural centre, community, whatever. I have since taken interviews with people about specific rooms in which women and girls were reportedly violated and there were reportedly beatings and killings. I did not get into wherever those rooms were. There was no sign, as I've testified and written, of any blood on walls or anything that I could see. Until we got the photographs that we were given that day. So it's difficult to answer the question exactly. There were clearly places that we didn't get to that I now know about, but we weren't, you know, hindered in our movements. And I don't know whether those rooms were in those two buildings or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there other buildings part of the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the rooms in which these episodes were said to have taken place were in those two buildings or in other buildings. There might have been places upstairs that we didn't get to. I didn't go up any stairs, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "other buildings," does that mean that other buildings were part of Trnopolje camp apart from the two main buildings, that there were more buildings which belonged to what you describe as the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as I know, to the best of my knowledge, the two buildings that you've described were the -- the main, as it were, built structures of the camp. But some -- or at least one of the violations that I've been told about took place, for instance, in an adjoining house. So one isn't quite sure where the frontier is, if you like. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, you have described the secluded part, fenced in the -- partly or not fenced in part. Was it clear where the boundaries of the camp were in general, and how would you know? If it's not fenced in...

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes, exactly. Thank you, Your Honour. Because with regard to the half of the camp that was fenced or partly fenced around the buildings, it was hard to judge where the boundary was. Particularly, as we've established, people could go scavenging for food, and there were violations, I now understand, in the house and adjoining. Very differently was that compound where the men had arrived from Keraterm. That was up against a wall on the side of the camp as we approached it from, I -- I'll work out -- I'll work out the direction if I think about a map. But that was a wall and three sides fencing, one of which was the barbed wire, and of that bit, of course, the compound was very clearly defined by the fencing and the guards around it and the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Let's have a look at the time. We are close to one hour. Would it be better to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That would probably be the best idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would request the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. And we resume at five minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could you inform us as to the time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, my best estimate is about maybe 30 minutes at the max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you'll now be re-examined by Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, on cross-examination, you were asked a series of questions regarding an incident which occurred on the way to Omarska involving gun-fire. Do you recall that line of questions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I believe in the transcript it was pages 2621 through 2637.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you were a shown a video which purported to depict the sounds of gun-fire. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now going to play two video-clips, first D43 which was introduced yesterday by Defence counsel. And like Defence counsel, we will be focussed on the ambient sounds. We will then play a segment from 65 ter 22615A.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I will ask Ms. Stewart first to play D43, and then to play 65 ter 22615A. I would ask you to listen very closely to the ambient sounds, not necessarily any words that might be on there. And for that, reason, Your Honours, I don't believe we need any translation. In the first clip, I particularly ask you to listen for sounds of gun-fire. After we've played both clips, I have some questions that I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart, for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D43 is still MFI'd, at this moment, but, of course, still can be played. And apparently, since we're supposed to ignore any spoken words, I suggest that we close our ears, apart from any fire exchanges, and that we do not need transcription or translation of any words spoken. And therefore we can play the video once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will ask Ms. Stewart to play D43, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll now ask Ms. Stewart to play 65 ter 22615A.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, were you present for the events that are visually depicted in both video-clips?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were located in the vehicles that we've seen in the video?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the same vehicle as Penny Marshall, the lady in the pink shirt, I think, the blonde lady, but I'm still sitting in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us, first, for the transcript record, could you please articulate a comparison of the two visual representations that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are of if not exactly the same scene more or less the same scene. One is obviously much more used than the other one. The first one is -- has been transferred from tape to tape and is of lower quality, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in the first tape, D43, could you describe for the record the ambient sounds towards the end of the clip?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I testified, I think, yesterday, on that clip, I can hear rapid and frequent fire quite like a battle, and as I testified yesterday a deep explosion from what sounded to me like heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you, were you describing the whole of the clip or as you were asked to do only the end of the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, sir. I think towards the end of the clip there is a rapid -- there is some rapid heavy fire, and then at the end of the clip -- towards the very end of the clip there's a deep explosion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the deep explosion is the part of the clip you were asked about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At the time that you were there on 5th of August, 1992, did you hear anything like the sounds that are reflected on D43?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I heard as I think I testified yesterday, sporadic rifle fire. But nothing of that depth or -- or ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then for the transcript record, could you describe the audio that you heard in the second clip from 65 ter 22615A.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident is fairly much over by then. If there is one shot, there is no more than one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And what is the predominant sound that we could here in the second clip?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's not much. I think there's an engine starting up or left running, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And is that consistent with your recollection of the sounds that you hard at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the sounds of the car at the time I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us, then, which of these videos accurately depicts the ambient sounds of the scene as you recall them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the second one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 22615A, and I can identify that this was -- or it is identified as coming from Serb Sarajevo television. It was disclosed on 10th February 2012 on a hard disc. And the spreadsheet indexed to that disclosure bundle indicated that this video is connected to Ed Vullimay as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, Madam Registrar, the second video, I take it that the surrogate sheet has been uploaded. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22615A becomes Exhibit P202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P202 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now like to play a segment as the Court had requested yesterday, 65 ter 22564A. The Chamber asked yesterday to look into whether or not a particular clip that was played as D263 had sound. The portions of that are -- the portion that was played is from an original compilation from the Tadic trial. We were able to find an original VHS in evidence and we have digitalised that. There is some sound on it. And for the matter of clarity, I would like to play that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I would like to invite the parties to see, because we'll have to carefully compare the two videos we have seen before, to see whether they can agree on whether certain portions of what is shown depict the same event by carefully comparing who moves, where, with what movement as far as body is concerned, or arms, so as to be assisted by the parties on whether there are, if not all, portions of the two videos where what is depicted is the identical moment an event so that it will be able to compare whether there's any difference in the sounds heard at this moment. Of course, the Chamber will also try to do its utmost best, but certainly would be assisted by the parties agreeing on -- if -- if there's a basis for agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position of the Prosecutor is that these two clips, D43 and I believe it's now P202, were identical footage from the same camera with different -- one being the original raw footage which is P202 and D43 having an audio track added on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is not exactly what I was seeking at this moment. But this is -- well, finally, if you agree on that we see is the same, of course, then the Chamber can compare what it hears.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Except that the -- this clip was from Serb TV Sarajevo -- Serb TV Sarajevo and the other one was from RTS, so I don't know yet, Your Honours, I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It looks to be similar shots, but I'm asking for the original tape from the provider of D43 to see if I can add more information. But visually the parts that are seen look the same, but I'm not -- I'm not able to say whether one is the original or one -- the raw footage. Raw footage is a very specific term. If it's broadcast, it's not raw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about which one is the original. What I'm seeking is that the two be compared and whoever broadcasted it, if the pictures are exactly the same, that means the same point of camera, the same movements of persons, then you can say since you cannot have two cameras before one eye, that most likely that comes from one camera and therefore is the same footage. Whoever may have worked on it, sound, et cetera, that is what the Chamber is seeking you to think about, whether what you see, and Ms. Bibles apparently has made up her mind on the matter already, but you also can agree. You cannot agree on your own, Ms. Bibles. You only can agree together with the Defence so that the Chamber is assisted in further analysing what exactly the potential issues are in relation to this video. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll ask Ms. Stewart now to play 65 ter 22564A.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vulliamy, I would ask you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, take your earphones off and lower your voice. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you hear in that clip any of the large loud shelling that we heard in D43?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would at this time proffer or tender 65 ter 22564A.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22564A becomes Exhibit P203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P203 is admitted into evidence. By the way, Ms. Bibles, I don't think that the witness used the word "shelling." He was talking about sound -- noises. But that's my recollection. I stand corrected if I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, and I -- the Court may have seen me pause as I tried to grab the exact phrase myself, so I may have been incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, going back to this event in your mind, what was your impression at the time of the purpose of this event? You've ...

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was hard to tell exactly, but we were under the impression they didn't really want us -- that the committee in Prijedor didn't really want us to go to go to Omarska. Indeed, they told us they'd rather we didn't go. But they were under Dr. Karadzic's orders, and as I think I testified, I was unconvinced by the nature of the supposed attack or exchange of fire. I think I testified that the shooting, such as it was, was going over our heads and the return fire was high. And men were -- they were, as we saw, scampering around, but they weren't diving for cover as one would if there was the kind of fire-fight going on for real. So I was unconvinced. I'm uncertain about this, but I think it was probably some kind of prank to dissuade us. But, as it turned out, we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to next turn to some questions you were asked on cross-examination with respect to white sheets or white flags.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I believe this line of questioning began at 2649, lines 18 to 14. You were asked about passing villages with white towels or flags hanging from the structures. Based on the interviews which you've conducted regarding people who put up the white sheets or the white towels, what is your understanding as to the choices that they truly faced in 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they could put up the white flags and accept that they would have to hand over their properties, leave - and it turned out to be via Trnopolje for enforced deportation - or face consequences as had been meted to other places like Kozarac, that their houses would be flattened and that they would, like many others, be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2649, Ms. Bibles, is? Is that today or yesterday's transcript? It couldn't be today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It was yesterday's transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid that I have not yet the -- but I'll find it. Thank you. We have -- I still have the old version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would you like me to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You were asked about the description that you had given in your article of 7 August 1992 describing that Trnopolje was not a concentration camp. Do you recall that line of questions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in your answer, you partially explained that your opinion regarding this conclusion changed during the convoy to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Your Honours, this was yesterday at 2666 I believe at lines 18 to 19, although that's -- those are the numbers that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about the experience, what experience in the convoy changed your opinion about Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although most of the people in the convoy had come from Sanski Most, there was a busload from Trnopolje, and the -- when we arrived Travnik, I realised the scale of what was happening and the regularity with which it was happening, that we were just one night among many, indeed every night, and the ferocity of what was happening because, as I ascertained quite soon afterwards, there had been a massacre four nights after our convoy on Mount Vlasic, known to this Tribunal as the Vlasic massacre. So in terms of Trnopolje, and its role, and the term "concentration camp" which I think I testified yesterday, I wanted to relate more to its South African origins than to the Third Reich, one realised -- at least I realised, directly, that the combination of the scale of these convoys of the enforced deportations, the regularity of them, every night, the numbers involved as were amassing in Travnik, something like 36.000 by the time we'd arrived and upon my return this got up into a -- into a much higher figures. Towards six figures. That Trnopolje was a kind of hub, a focal point for the internment of these people, civilians, family, children, old people - and there's no distinction here - for enforced deportations on convoys of the kind that I was on. I've testified in the evidence before about what it was like to be on that convoy. I don't need to take your time now with how terrifying it was. It was old people, children, someone in a wheelchair going over the rocks in the road, for instance, and it became quickly clear soon afterwards that Trnopolje was the focal point, the hub, the point of departure for the vast majority or -- not the vast but the majority of people in this systematic enforced deportation either that camp or directly, as in the case of those from Sanski Most, from their homes. So it was the experience of the convoy, the arrival in Travnik, subsequent visits to Travnik, and over the past 20 years very extensive interviews with people with who have shared that road that this was the purpose or one of the purposes of Trnopolje, as we also know many were killed, raped, or beaten while they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in the same vein, based on all of the experiences and work that you've just described, do you have an understanding as to what choices were available in 1992 to members of non- -- or to non-Serb leaders and professionals in those communities?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got a glimpse of this on the day, on the 5th of August, when it became clear that the leaders of opposition parties were in Omarska. We were introduced to the leader of the SDA, which was a pro-Muslim party. And I've -- it became quite quickly clear that members of, if I like, the intelligentsia, the political leadership, the local elite, were quickly earmarked for persecution, death, and actually there was a -- if the Court would permit me, there was a sort of a perverse pecking order in the violation of the women as I later established that, for instance, the camp commander Mijakic had to "have" a lady, who was the leader of the Croatian party. So the higher up the pecking order you were in the guards, the higher up the pecking order you, as it were, got the lady, for want of a better way of putting that. So, yes, there was a targeting of the intelligentsia, of the doctors, the educated people, without doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that concludes my re-direct examination of Mr. Vulliamy. With respect to the matter -- sorry. Your Honours, in terms of associated exhibits, at this point I've decided not to tender 65 ter 17933 [sic], 17995, 18001, 22365A, and 22573. I would tendered the remainder of the associated exhibits which have not been entered yet. With respect to 17992, which is the article used by the Defence, I would tender that at this time, as well as 22572 and 22393A. And I do note here that the 92 ter filing for this witness indicated the relevant parts of the Stakic testimony in which these exhibits were referred to by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to the associated exhibits, Your Honour, although I do note that I think counsel misspoke as to one. I think it's 17993. It has been recorded in the transcript as 17933 at line 25. Yeah. Of the previous page. And then I would have one question in re-cross-examination that arises out of the re-direct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first check. So three associated exhibits. Now, I'm looking at my list, 22393A was not on my -- perhaps I am using an old list. Yes, I see I'm using the wrong list. Let me check. So we have three associated exhibits. No objections, Mr. Ivetic? I'd rather first deal with it administratively --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise it remains... Madam Registrar 17992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. P -- 22393A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 22572.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, today when you were viewing these new clips that the Office of the Prosecution had of the convoy, at page 56, line 1 of the transcript, you indicated the incident was fairly over by then. Am I to understand your testimony that the shooting that you remember would have been before the point in time that we saw the clips today?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness. But for the record, Your Honour, the disclosure for this witness on May the 4th, 2012, the 40 exhibits does not include 22615A.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We did not intend to introduce that video-clip. We were aware that the witness testified about what he has referred to as a prank in the Stakic testimony. We did not intend to raise that in direct. It was not until the Defence introduced D43 yesterday that we then went back to the videos that we had disclosed with respect to the sounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not have a D43 available before?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We did not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These circumstances justify why you had not notified at an earlier stage the Defence of the use of these videos. Then I think we have... yes. Mr. Ivetic, I think that yesterday, when you tendered 1D263, a video, we ended up in a discussion about surrogate sheets well or not being uploaded and that finally no number has been assigned to it. Therefore, I take it that we have to finalise that as well. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D263 becomes Exhibit D46, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D46. Was there any objection? Ms. Bibles. Just I have to ... that was the first video played yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was just wanting to double-check my numbers. That is virtually identical to P203. This is the video that was silent yesterday and we've also introduced the sound. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D46 is admitted into evidence. Then for D43, it was MFI'd. There was some -- let me just check with Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D43 remains marked for identification because there was some technical problem with what was actually on the DVD or CD that was provided, so that will be resolved but for the time being it remains marked for identification. Having dealt with that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record we would object to D43 or any of the material from the emperorsclothes or referred to that way coming into evidence. It's our position that D43 - in fact, the audio track - was doctored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that ... isn't it true that D46 was taken from the same source?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And I think -- I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Now, the record says this was the video that was silent. Objection. I may have misheard you. I thought you said there was no objection, but otherwise my response was should have caused all kind of problems. Did you object earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually, I may need to go back and take a look at these. I believe that D46 and P203 are virtually identical, and I did not object to D46. If I was acting in mistake, I will bring that to the Trial Chamber's attention at a later date. I will go take a closer look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please take a closer look at it. Then, Mr. Ivetic, any other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not from my side, Your Honour. That was what I was going to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vulliamy, this then concludes your testimony in this court. Perhaps I should say at least in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thank you for coming to The Hague for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return -- well, or at least a safe travel to wherever you will travel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Home, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, very much indeed for your time. I'm most grateful for your time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? I have been considered whether or not to take a break now. That would be a break until ten minutes past 1.00. We would then have 65 further minutes. Perhaps that's the best way to proceed. I see everyone, including the accused, nodding yes so that we don't have to interrupt the testimony of that witness. And that witness was scheduled for how long, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One hour examination, I believe, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So most likely we will be able to conclude the examination-in-chief today so that cross-examination can start tomorrow. We take a break and we resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Ibro Osmanovic, RM067.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to give the decision of the Chamber on the request, the permission to reply to the response to the 92 ter motion for this witness. That request is granted, and we have received the reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is brought in, first of all I will address a matter with regard to the 92 ter statement to be tendered with the witness. Upon further review, the Prosecution will use as 92 ter material only the 65 ter 28376, which is the witness statement of 10 October 1994; and the 65 ter 28377, which is the supplemental statement of 11 October 1995. Second point. Maybe I can refer to the relevant adjudicated facts for this testimony, which are from 505 to 516, from 1241 to 1250, and then 1261 to 1265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Osmanovic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, you will first be examined by Ms. D'Ascoli. Ms. D'Ascoli is counsel for the Prosecution and you will find her to your right. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ibro Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, do you remember providing a statement to the ICTY on 5, 7, and 10 October 1994?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28376 on the screens. This is a statement of Mr. Osmanovic signed on the 10th of October, 1994. And, Your Honours, I want to mention that we have uploaded a version of this statement which has a -- a numbered paragraph both in B/C/S and in English. Of course, we have communicated to the Defence and they had no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, if you can have -- if you can look at the English of the statement. In particular, the signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we can have a look at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether you recognise that signature.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we then go at the last page, which is page 17 of the -- does this work? No. I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I don't -- I don't think it's the microphone. It must be something else because my microphone doesn't produce any sound either.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The connection seems ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think now --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Now it works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We resume after this technical problem. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think I asked to go to the last page of the English document, which is page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, again, sir, I asked you if you recognise the signature which is on top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So if you can move on top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I will now deal with a couple of corrections that you wanted to make to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we move to page 5 of this statement - this is page 4 -- page 5 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if you could look at the very first line of paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe we can zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I understand there was a correction that you wanted to make with regard to the third person listed here. Can you tell us what the correction is?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's Zoran's son, Goran. The correction, as far as the last name is concerned, is that the surname should be Deuric. Deuric. In fact, here it says "Djuric," so the correct surname is Deuric.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So do I understand correctly that the full name, the correct one should read Goran Deuric, which was son of Zoran, right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to please spell the last name of this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, could you please spell the last name of this person?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Goran, G-o-r-a-n.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The last name, please. The family name.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: D-e-u-r-i-c, with a diacritic mark on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we can now go to page 6. And zoom in on the very first line of paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, you wanted to make a correction also to the name mentioned here. Can you please tell us what that correction is?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It had to do with the name, since there are two brothers Miljanici. There is Slavisa and I can't remember the other one. It only concerns -- the correction only concerns the name Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, in proofing you said the name was not Slavisa but Sinisa, correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were the two Miljanic brothers, so the correction only concerns the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Exactly. So -- in paragraph 21 you meant to refer to Sinisa Miljanic; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Taking into account these changes, are you satisfied that this statement is an accurate record of what happened and what you experienced as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now -- can I now ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28377, and this is the supplemental statement signed on 11 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, again, can I ask you to view the first page of the English document, in particular the signature at the bottom of the page, and please indicate whether you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we then go to the last page of the English document, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And again, I ask you whether you recognise the signature at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, are you satisfied that this supplemental statement is an accurate record of what happened and what you experienced as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This supplemental statement relates to Gertbakovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter heard the name correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, can you please repeat? You said that the supplemental statement relates to ...

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: To the Batkovici camp near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, subject to the corrections that we discussed for the previous statement, if the Chamber takes these two statements together, will it have a correct picture of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if you were asked today the same questions that you were asked during those interviews in 1994 and 1995, would you keep the same answers and provide the same information in substance?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir, now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm that you have provided that information in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders the 65 ter 28376 and 28377, pursuant to Rule 92 ter as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Defence. I don't know yet who to address, but Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any objections Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 28376 would become.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 28377.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Now, with the Chamber's permission I would briefly summarise Mr. Osmanovic evidence for the record and for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you have explained to Mr. Osmanovic the purpose of reading out so that the public is aware of what is in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Ibro Osmanovic is a Bosnian Muslim from Vlasenica who was detained during 1992 and 1993 in the Vlasenica police station, the Vlasenica municipality prison, Susica camp and Batkovic camp. He testifies about how the JNA took over the most vital departments in the town of Vlasenica on 23, 24 April 1992. On 22 May 1992, the witness was arrested and detained with other Muslim men in the police station at Vlasenica. This began a period of detention that lasted from May 1992 until July 1993 in different detention facilities. From the Vlasenica police station, the witness was transferred to the Vlasenica municipality prison, then the Susica camp, and finally Batkovic camp in Bijeljina where the witness ultimately remained until he was released in July 1993. While detained at Vlasenica municipality prison in June 1992, the witness was taken with other prisoners to the Muslim settlement of Drum, a suburb of Vlasenica, to bury bodies. He buried 22 bodies. Of all those men, all but one had single gun-shot wounds between their eyes. The witness provides evidence of beatings and mistreatments at Susica camp, a facility commanded by Dragan [realtime transcript read in error "Drago"] Nikolic, and he also testifies about beatings and killings of the detainees held at Batkovic where the witness was moved at end of June 1992. And that concludes the summary of the evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you for the clarity of the transcript. You mentioned a name in page 76, line 9. Is that properly recorded, Ms. D'Ascoli?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That should be Dragan Nikolic. I see that it is written Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also have a question to clarify. At page 75, line 19, you're saying that in Vlasenica police station the Vlasenica municipality prison Susica camp and Batkovici camp, and then you don't -- you mention the name of the army that brought the witness to those places but it's -- what was the name of the army?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I said that he testifies about how the JNA took over the most vital departments in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, now that I read the summary of your evidence, I'm going to ask you some questions to clarify or expand upon that evidence. First of all, do you know approximately how many inhabitants the town of Vlasenica had in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Vlasenica had approximately 10.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: What about the town, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The town of Vlasenica itself had between 4- and 5.000 inhabitants, if you include the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I understand from your statement, the 1994 one, at paragraph 10, that in April and May 1992, the Muslim population of Vlasenica was not allowed to move freely within the municipality or to leave it if they were not issued with specific passes for that purpose, and you also specify in the same paragraph that the passes to leave the town were issued by the crisis committee of Vlasenica. Now as you mention in that paragraph only the Muslim population, I take it that this procedure did not apply also to the -- did not apply to the Serb population; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim population moved around having obtained passes issued by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica. On the other hand, the Serbian population could move around freely without such passes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer to call up 65 ter 02862, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, in the same paragraph 10 of your statement, you also tell that one time you were issued with one of such passes to go visit your brother. Now, can you please look at the original of this document. Did you have chance of reviewing it during proofing -- during preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a pass in which passage to Zivinice is authorised. This is -- these are certificates that were issued for people who were leaving Vlasenica, and it was a pass or a certificate issued to Remzija Huric.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And is this pass similar to the one that was issued to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But where it says "we hereby authorise a trip to Zivinice," in my case it concerned a trip from Vlasenica to Bregovi where the family has a house, and I was enabled or allowed to go to Piskavice.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And whose signature was on the pass that was issued to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Milenko Stanic signed it. And Matic signed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And sir, what is the signature that you see on this pass; and is that similar or the same as the one that was on your pass?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Milenko Stanic signed, but Matic signed on his behalf in the same way that he signed for everyone else, and that was also the case for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it, your pass, with regard to the signature, it looked exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I tender this document, 65 ter 02862 into evidence as a public exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02862 becomes Exhibit P209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P209 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I will now move to your detention in the municipality, in the Vlasenica municipality prison. At paragraph 28 of your 1994 statement, which is now P207, you describe how during your detention at the Vlasenica municipality prison you were taken to Drum to bury bodies and that you buried 22 bodies there. Can you tell me by whom you were taken to Drum?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: People from the police station in Vlasenica took us to Drum. People in uniform of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And this happened while you were detained at the Vlasenica municipality prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And this was in June 1992. Do you remember more or less when in June?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June I was transferred to the municipal prison from the police station, so that was at the very beginning. It could have been on the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: With regard to the -- to the bodies that you buried, what type of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Meaning you had -- meaning -- you mean that they had civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And what was their age group, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were between 20 and 60 years of age, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in the same paragraph, sir, you mention that you knew four of these 22 bodies; namely, Ekrim Jahic, his father Abdullah Jahic, Nedzad Odic, and Osmo Odic. Can you tell us what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They are people I knew, and they were of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you know if also the other bodies were of the same ethnicity, Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because that settlement was inhabited exclusively by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you know if these bodies were ever exhumed from there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were moved from that place, but I do know that they were buried in the Sehiski [as interpreted] cemetery in Vlasenica, after the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the cemetery where you buried them in -- in Drum? You mention -- you described it as being near the "boksit" stadium?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, behind the "boksit" stadium there's the Muslim cemetery Roblejakita [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And is this a different cemetery from the previous one you mentioned, the Sehiski cemetery in Vlasenica? And I'm sorry for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Sehici [as interpreted] cemetery was created after the war. People who had been found in mass graves would be buried there as martyrs, people who had been killed in Vlasenica were subsequently buried there. In the Rakite cemetery, well, that cemetery was used to bury people as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. One last question with regard to this area of your testimony. Is the Dzamdzici village close to the village of Drum?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Dzamdzici village is in the immediate vicinity just across the hill behind Drum village.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I will now move to the Susica camp. You were transferred to Susica camp on 18 June 1992. And this is paragraph 31 of P207. Were you ever told why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And later on at paragraph 32, you say that when you arrived into the hangar at Susica, there were about 500 to 550 people there. And you saw also people that you knew from -- from Vlasenica and surrounding villages. So of the men that you personally knew in Susica camp, were any of them involved, as far as you know, in any subversive or violent activities of any kind?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Because there was no armed conflict in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 37 of your 1994 statement, you describe how two detainees, Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic, two pensioners that you knew, they were taken out of the hangar by Dragan Nikolic on 22 June 1992. I want to show you a document with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 19197. And this is a report by prison warden Veljko Basic, dated the 22nd of June 1992 concerning the deaths of Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic at Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at the original of this document. Did you have a chance of reviewing it in the preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please -- can you please have a look at the description of the cause of death for these two men and tell us if what you read in the document concerning the deaths of these two men corresponds to what you saw?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did they die of heart attack, as this document states?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They died because of beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And was there -- was any medical examination ever done on the bodies of these two people at the camp, as far as you saw, because you were in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Hadzic died right next to me. He was lying by my legs. And there was no examination carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: What about the second person?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Zildzic died during the night as soon as they brought him back after the beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, according also to what you saw happened after their deaths, can you tell us if you think that they could have been buried according to Muslim customs as this document says for both bodies?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe they were only taken to the Muslim cemetery and buried there, but they certainly were not buried in accordance with Muslim rites.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And does of the date of this document, the 22nd of June, correspond to your recollection concerning when these two men died?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the date tallies, the 22nd. However, this does not tally, what Veljko Basic said, that they were examined by a physician and buried in accordance with Muslim rites.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you know the person who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Veljko Basic, retired policeman, acquitted by the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina on account of his advanced age. He was commander of the camp in Susica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you remove this exhibit from the screen, ma'am. Can we just establish from Mr. Osmanovic what is the family name of Asim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Asim Zildzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 19917 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19917 becomes Exhibit P210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, in several paragraphs of your statement, for example paragraph 37, 39, 42, or 44 of P207, you describe episodes of men who were taken out of the hangar and beaten. On the basis of what you observed and experienced, would you say that beatings were frequent or not at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that they were frequent. Some people were actually beaten every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in your statement you also describe episodes of killings or of men who died after being taken out of the hangar and beaten. Can I ask you what was the ethnicity of all these detainees who were beaten and/or killed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, on the basis of what you observed and experienced in Susica camp, why do you think Bosnian Muslims were detained, beaten, and/or killed in Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness would have to speculate in order to answer a question that was phrased this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, could you please rephrase your question such that we know what -- on what facts the witness -- whatever opinion he may have formed, bases it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, during your detention at Susica camp, on the basis of the beatings or the killings or -- of what you saw was happening to Bosnian Muslim detainees, were you able to -- to form or to develop an idea or did you -- did you become aware of the reason why this was happening?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite simply all the beatings that happened to a certain group of people, all this torture that we suffered at the hands of our neighbours, until that day, no one could really figure this out. No one was guilty of anything. I lived in my own house. I was taken out of my house. And I was taken out there. The same thing happened to all my neighbours. Unfortunately, these people who were killed are no longer with us. They were accused of all sorts of things. One of them was accused of having manufactured knives, another one of smuggling. However, since he couldn't move about anywhere, I don't see how he could have smuggling. Also the one who was accused of making knives. When was he making these knives? So it was sufficient to pin something on someone and then they would experience what we experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you already said that you were not given a reason for being detained. In so far as you know, were the people you knew there at the camp, were they ever told why they were detained?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. On one occasion, they came and said that we would be exchanged for some detained Serbs who were allegedly grazing grass at the stadium in Tuzla. We received the same information in Batkovic once as well. However, we never found out what the actual reason for our detention was.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I will now move to your detention in Batkovic. You were transferred there on the 30th of June, 1992, and you spent more than a year in this camp. Are you able to give an estimate for what you saw of how many persons approximately were detained there at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When the Batkovic camp was established, the first group was brought in from Vlasenica on the 27th, the second one on the 28th, and I arrived in the third group on the 30th of the June. In Vlasenica there were between 500 and 550 of us. Four hundred had already arrived in Batkovic once I got there, because one group stayed on in Vlasenica. After that, people were brought in from the area of the municipality of Zvornik, from the area of the municipality of Brcko, from the area of the municipality of Lopare, Ugljevik, also from the area of the municipality of Rogatica. Today my estimate would be that at full capacity there were 3.500 of us in this camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, did you know many of the -- many people among the detainees there at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The people who arrived from Vlasenica, I knew them, 90 per cent of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I now want to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If the Court Officer, please, if they can call up P191.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of a list of persons detained at Batkovic stamped and certified on by the Bijeljina lower court as being identical to the original. And for each name, it lists last name, father's name, first name, date and place of birth, residence, date and time of arrival, the collection centre, and date and time of departure from the collection centre. Mr. Osmanovic, did you have a chance of reviewing in detail this document in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you remember seeing on this document names that you recognised where -- of people detained with you at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 138 of the original of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can look at entry number 21.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, and you also said that you recognised when you reviewed this rather long list, you were able to recognise many other persons listed in this document because they were detained there with you at Batkovic. I will just mention a couple of examples. For example, in your statement you mentioned a man called Fadil Halilhodzic at paragraphs 60 and 62 of P207. This man was singled out for beatings several times and he belonged to a group called the special prisoners, because they were often singled out for beatings. Do you remember seeing his name on this list?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, this is entry number 38 on page 3 of the original document, P191.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, further in your statement, paragraph 39 of P207, you also refer to someone by the name of Reuf Rasidagic who was beaten by Dragan Nikolic about five times over four or five days, and eventually begged Nikolic to kill him. Do you remember seeing his name on this list?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Rasidagic, Reuf. He was beaten up - he wasn't killed - by Dragan Nikolic at the Susica camp. He kicked him and he also hit him with his rifle, and he said to him, lie to me, telling me when you were last in a cinema. It's expensive to waste a bullet on you. Three marks per bullet. Tell me where your brother is. That was the reason why he beat him. And Reuf did arrive alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you remember seeing also his name on this list?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And for the record, this is entry number 18 on page 151 of the original document, P191. Finally, if we can go to page 164 of the original, please. And if we can have a look at entry number 98.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me if you recognise this name, entry 98?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Smajic Age Ejub from Bijeljina was beaten to death in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm done with the document. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, at paragraph 61 of P207, and then more extensively in your 1995 statement, which is P208, you tell about three detainees who appear to be willing participants in the beatings of other detainees and who would beat the other detainees with our without the presence of the guards. Now, my question is: How did the guards react when seeing such beatings from detainees on other detainees?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They laughed and they approved of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did they do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: To stop them? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, as far as you know, did any guard or other prison officials that you heard of suggest the possibility that anyone would be punished for participating in the beatings of other detainees?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, and, again, with regard to the Batkovic camp, in several paragraphs of your statement, paragraphs 54 to 60, for example, you describe episodes of men who were taken out of the hangar and beaten; and also at paragraph 57 of the 1994 statement you also describe how an old man, Zulfo Hadziomerovic, died as a result of the beatings. Now, on the basis of what you saw, what you observed there at the camp, would you say that beatings were frequent or not, at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Beatings were a daily thing. It was like a daily meal for a group of specials.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the detainees who were beaten and/or killed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats. Croats arrived once the Brcko camp had been closed down. Before that, there were only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere there in the camp? Were you scared?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: An atmosphere of fear. Everyone was in fear for their own lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, I also want to ask you some questions about your family. Did you lose any family members in 1992/1993 after the takeover of Vlasenica town?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lost three members of my family, my immediate family, and a total of 36 relatives from my extended family. I lost two brothers and a sister. The sister was 16 years old. She was burned to death. She was found at the location of Pelemis in the municipality of Sekovici. Only 7 per cent of her mortal remains were found. My younger brother was found in the area of Kljestani of the municipality of Vlasenica. Three mass graves were discovered, and his head was found 25 kilometres away. As for my older brother, nothing has been found yet. I cannot find any trace whatsoever. So these are members of my very own family, from my very own home. Also my maternal uncle and his family, all of them are missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you tell me the name of your younger sister, the sister who was 16 years old?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ferida.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you clarify the circumstances of her death, if you know, what happened?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mother was in camp and the sisters were sent to Cerska. She was a child and she got lost in the woods and was lost somewhere in the area of the Serb positions. Then she was returned to the Susica camp again. So the last traces led to Pelemis in the municipality of Sekovici. She was found this year. She was buried on the 24th -- or, rather, funeral services were held at the Muslim cemetery of martyrs. There were only 7 per cent of her mortal remains were found, unfortunately. All the rest were burned. At this funeral service, most of the persons buried were young girls. None of them were even 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: To clarify in the record, I see that her name is recorded as Ferid. Sir, can you repeat her first name?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ferida.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness said that only 7 per cent of her remains were found. This in correction to page 90, line 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
